What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1676 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jamal Musiala came off the bench with 14 minutes remaining in Bayern's defeat by Lille on Wednesday.
  • Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.
  • During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jamal Musiala came off the bench with 14 minutes remaining in Bayern's defeat by Lille on Wednesday.

Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players - have collided over recent weeks.

During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.

This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.

At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.

But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".

In a recent development, in April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.

According to recent reports, nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.

Sources indicate that soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an matter. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.

After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.

However, his comeback lasted just two games - he came off the bench in Bayern's 1-1 Bundesliga draw against Cologne, and in the Champions League defeat by Lille, but the club confirmed on Friday that he has torn his right hamstring and will be out until further notice.

Recent findings suggest that on top of that, newly introduced incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training, Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.

All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.

It has been revealed that absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.

Recent findings suggest that A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.

The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.

"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge remarked. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer.".

A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.

Hoffmann, a neurologist, remarked it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.

One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.

He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.

But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.

Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.

It has been revealed that musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.

Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.

Recent findings suggest that under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, Â£21m a year, with Â£15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to Â£25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.

It has been revealed that some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract only offers sick pay for six weeks before insurance would shoulder the payments.

But even six months is a short period in comparison. Premier League players receive their full basic wage for the first 18 months. And, when Bayern negotiate with top players, they ultimately compete against Europe's elite.

Rummenigge, and to a lesser extent his long-time boardroom compatriot Uli Hoeness, made Eberl responsible for the unfavourable terms - arguing that Schmid essentially played Eberl.

Eberl has been the target of criticism from the two former powerbrokers for quite some time. At a recent supervisory board meeting, Hoeness is stated to have attacked Eberl for his inactivity over the Musiala concern in the past six months.

That being mentioned, Bayern bought into the Musiala hype for a couple of years, hoping that they would have a superstar of their own who could be marketed across the globe.

Industry observers note that the relationship between the club and agent Schmid has been strained to say the least, with Rummenigge particularly disliking him. Some sources believe this was one of the root causes for Rummenigge's recent attack on live TV.

When a 16-year-old Kennet Eichhorn came on the market during the summer, as he wanted to leave second-division side Hertha Berlin, Bayern were interested but ultimately dropped out of the race for the highly touted midfielder. Eichhorn is represented by Schmid and ended up joining Bayer Leverkusen.

Bayern boss Vincent Kompany (left) has himself recently been diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

According to recent reports, hoeness met with Schmid during the summer to discuss how to proceed with Musiala, but the player's agent did not indicate that they would agree to a wage reduction. Hoeness called the matter a "dilemma" for Bayern during a TV show earlier this month, but did not go as far as Rummenigge.

As long as Musiala is not medically forced to retire, he will receive the wage that was agreed upon in February 2025. Even if Bayern would intend to part ways with the player, they would need to do everything in their power to get the player as close to his previous form as possible.

In a recent development, the release clause of Â£125m, which could be triggered next year, seems unrealistic. Any comments by Bayern bosses against Musiala, or further leaks to the media, may indeed lower his market value down to zero - unless the player can simply shake things off and perform again.

According to recent reports, eberl and head coach Vincent Kompany have come out to back Musiala. Joshua Kimmich, one of Bayern's veteran players, also criticised the treatment of Musiala after a 2-1 loss to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday. "Of course, the club is above all and bigger than the player, but not bigger than the human. This is an absolute no-go and also not Bayern-like," Kimmich noted.

Even football players' union Fifpro condemned Rummenigge's comments. On Wednesday, Bayern put out a statement saying that a meeting between the club and Musiala's representatives took place on Tuesday, in which it was agreed that the player's health should be paramount.

In a recent development, whether the damage can be repaired is up in the air. As Bayern have a number of attacking players sidelined, they need a healthy and mentally prepared Musiala in the coming weeks and months.

Industry observers note that imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

It has been revealed that now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising newly introduced direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

According to recent reports, to understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold.

In a recent development, superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a latest class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an vital advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," notes Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.".

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature.

The newly introduced study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

Sources indicate that "This is really good news," indicates Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.".

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together.

Recent findings suggest that superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

According to recent reports, in conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The newly introduced findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

Sources indicate that "The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," indicates Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.".

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.".

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue.

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

In a recent development, unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

Recent findings suggest that the findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for it breaking financial rules, senior figures at some Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.
  • This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The independent commission is yet to decide on a sanction for Manchester City.

Manchester City's owners must be forced to sell up as punishment for it breaking financial rules, senior figures at some Premier League clubs have told BBC Sport.

This week, the chair of the Independent Football Regulator (IFR) David Kogan claimed he has the "stomach" to take action against City, who deny wrongdoing and have appealed.

The IFR has the power to remove directors of a club if they are deemed unsuitable, and even force a sale in the most serious cases.

Now, officials at three top-flight clubs have told the BBC that they believe this is the appropriate punishment for City, who were found guilty of breaching Premier League financial regulations between 2009 and 2018, and failing to co-operate with an investigation.

Premier League clubs to cover legal costs if Man City sponsors sue.

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City.

The independent commission has yet to decide on a sanction that could range from a fine, to a points deduction, the stripping of past titles, or even expulsion from the league.

According to recent reports, but speaking on condition of anonymity, one executive claimed they are among a group of clubs who feel that City's punishment will be irrelevant unless the owners are also forced to sell. They added that anything less will make them question why they are funding the regulator through a levy.

In comments that reveal the level of anger felt by other clubs, another source claimed the rule breaches had undermined the league's credibility, and that they would not be able to draw a line under the scandal and move on if the owners were allowed to stay. The club were found guilty of inflating revenues and disguising losses by Â£900m through "sham" commercial arrangements.

Manchester City's owners are Abu Dhabi United Group - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president and deputy Prime Minister Sheikh Mansour.

Sources indicate that the official - who also spoke anonymously - mentioned that clubs had been asked by the Premier League to refrain from publicly revealing their views on sanctions, and let the process run its course, although some are said to have privately made their opinions clear to IFR officials. They acknowledged that some clubs were less opinionated about a punishment.

Other clubs the BBC approached declined to comment, or mentioned they were willing for the independent commission panel and IFR to reach their own conclusions following the publication of the commission's ruling in September.

But the fact that some clubs want the unprecedented sanction of a forced sale will put pressure on Kogan to mete out the harshest penalty possible in what is being seen as a defining test of the watchdog just over a year after it was established.

It also comes amid mounting questions over whether wider UAE trade and investment in UK projects could be impacted by such a move. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club, adding that "they have been such a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester".

When approached, the IFR declined to comment. But Kogan has consistently noted that the IFR will not be influenced by any political pressure.

Earlier this week he told a parliamentary committee that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate City's hierarchy and take action, depending on the outcome of the appeal.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the glitch. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," Kogan said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so... assuming those circumstances are triggered, if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?".

Sheikh Mansour's control of Manchester City has come into question.

When asked how any potential legal battles with Manchester City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks told MPs that a litigation reserve of Â£2m was to be built up over the next two years via the levy charged to clubs, which would be paid back if litigation was successful.

Recent findings suggest that "Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than Â£2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular", Monks added. "So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.

It has been revealed that "We'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way.".

Last month it was revealed that the IFR would cost clubs in the top five divisions of English men's football Â£20.3m annually.

Last week, Premier League clubs voted to cover legal expenses for its five board directors if any of City's sponsors sued them. Two UAE-based commercial partners - Etihad and Etisalat - have both said they are considering legal action against the Premier League.

Industry observers note that the IFR has the authority to force a sale within section 34 of the Football Governance Act which allows it to investigate whether an owner meets the required suitability standards around honest, integrity and financial soundness. If an owner fails this assessment, the regulator can direct them to take reasonable steps to relinquish ownership within a specified period before issuing an ownership removal order.

City have been approached for comment. The club previously said that the commission's ruling contained "clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe", adding that they filed "a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence [that] exists in support of all of its positions".

More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1085 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • In a recent development, A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but latest research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

In a recent development, A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

According to recent reports, normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

It has been revealed that yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

Sources indicate that one of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath latest deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

It has been revealed that according to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. Fresh sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly crucial finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

According to recent reports, this agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Garnacho has not played for Aston Villa since making a three-minute cameo in a 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.

Aston Villa boss Unai Emery has praised Alejandro Garnacho's "fantastic attitude" -but suggested other players rank ahead of him after the Argentine was left out of Tuesday's Champions League defeat at Galatasaray.

The 22-year-old winger joined Aston Villa on loan from Chelsea in the summer, but he has played just 34 minutes in the Premier League this season.

Garnacho was left at home for the 2-0 loss by Galatasaray, with Emery bringing 11 substitutes - including two goalkeepers - rather than the maximum 12.

"When he is not involved in the squad it is because I have to choose with other players as well," said the Villa boss on Friday.

"He has my respect first as a person and second as a player, but he is not involved for this reason.

Industry observers note that "But football can change. We are playing matches so I will need players.".

Not even making a 12-man bench - what next for Garnacho?

Garnacho has played in just four of Villa's 11 Premier League matches this season and has yet to start across all competitions, coming off the bench for all seven of his appearances.

His last appearance - just a three-minute cameo - came in the 1-1 draw against Fulham on 31 October.

"Alejandro Garnacho is training very well. His attitude is fantastic, very good attitude," Emery added.

Recent findings suggest that "He was struggling at the beginning of the season because he was not fit. Now he is fit and he's training at a good level.".

Sources have acknowledged Garnacho was not at the level required and were surprised how off the pace he was when he signed in July.

He initially trained on his own, while his problems were not helped by a head injury suffered in Thailand in pre-season.

"Of course now he, and other players as well, are performing well, they are working well, they understood how we are building the squad," Emery stated.

"It's not how it was two months ago when he wasn't fit enough to be playing with the consistency we needed.

"So keep going, keep moving forward as a club, as a team, he himself as a player and we will see it.".

Garnacho's move to Villa will become permanent for Â£43m at the end of the season should certain criteria be met, but there are concerns his time at the club could become similar to that of Harvey Elliot, who played just nine times last season after arriving on loan from Liverpool.

Fifa rules allow players to play for two clubs in a season - or three if they move to a team whose season overlaps like the Major League Soccer - meaning Garnacho could feature for another team, unlike Elliott as he had already played for Liverpool and Villa.

Recent findings suggest that however, Emery stated he was not thinking about the upcoming January transfer window as he added: "It is November, of course there is a transfer window in January, but we are not thinking about the transfer window in January. Me especially.".

Does this damage Villa after Elliott lost a year of his career last season?

There was already talk in the game of how players could be fearful it could happen to them - and that caution may increase with Garnacho's situation.

Having happened twice in two seasons it would also leave clubs with second thoughts too given the players are their assets.

Garnacho has managed just 95 minutes across all competitions, having joined Villa to revive a faltering career after an inconsistent first season at Chelsea.

Head of football operations Damian Vidagany was unrepentant when asked about the winger at a fans' forum on Thursday, with Emery's trusted lieutenant fiercely backing the manager's judgement call.

Villa, though, arguably need a player like Garnacho - who can produce moments of magic like his stunning goal for Manchester United against Everton in 2023 - having failed to score in four of their last six winless games.

Emery wanted a pacy winger in the summer and the Argentine had been on their wanted list all year.

They need some need some creativity, so with Emery, at least publicly, refusing to rule out a January departure there could still be a slim chance of redemption.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, well, NASA astronaut Anil Menon will, anyway.
  • According to recent reports, "We need plants to survive as we set up our moon base, and as we go to Mars, we're going to have to grow our own nutrition.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The astronauts on the International Space Station will celebrate Thanksgiving with some nontraditional fare.

In a recent development, well, NASA astronaut Anil Menon will, anyway. In a video the agency released on Monday (Nov. 23), Menon demonstrated off some of the plants he and his crewmates are growing in orbit and told us what's in store for the greens.

According to recent reports, "We need plants to survive as we set up our moon base, and as we go to Mars, we're going to have to grow our own nutrition. So that's what we're doing this Thanksgiving," Menon mentioned in the 2.5-minute video.

In a recent development, "I plan on using this [plant] with a tortilla and some pasta and some hot sauce to make my Thanksgiving meal," added Menon, who was wearing a chef's toque for the occasion. "And I'm grateful for you and for my family at home.".

He passed the microphone to fellow NASA astronaut Luke Delaney, who didn't talk about food but expressed gratitude to his family, crewmates and support network on Earth.

Next up was NASA's Jessica Watkins, who gave us a rundown of the broader Thanksgiving menu in space.

"Some of what we'll be eating here — we've got some roasted turkey, some mac and cheese, some mashed potatoes, and some candied yams," Watkins noted, showing off the small bags containing each of those comestibles. "So, we should be in good shape.".

The Canadian Space Agency's (CSA) Joshua Kutryk spoke next. He noted he'll eat rice and the space-grown plants, which he'll consume raw "because it reminds me of Earth, which I miss.".

All four of the astronauts then wished us a happy Thanksgiving and did some zero-g flips and rolls, sending the space plants on a bit of a ride.

It has been revealed that delaney, Kutryk and Watkins are members of SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which arrived at the International Space Station (ISS) on Oct. 1. There's a fourth Crew-13 astronaut as well — Sergey Teteryatnikov, of the Russian space agency Roscosmos.

That quartet shares the ISS with Menon and cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, who arrived in July aboard a Russian Soyuz spacecraft.

In a recent development, astronauts tend to get major holidays off on the ISS, and to celebrate them together. Doing so reinforces the already-strong bonds the crewmates share and helps them deal with the pain of being away from friends and family, which can be especially acute on holidays like Thanksgiving and Christmas.

It has been revealed that kutryk is likely feeling especially emotional these days. On Tuesday, the CSA unveiled that Kutryk's wife had given birth to the couple's third child, a daughter.

Industry observers note that "Even with the distance between us, we feel incredibly connected as we welcome our latest little star into our lives," the couple stated in a statement shared by the CSA. "We are very proud of our growing family and are looking forward to getting our little crew of five all reunited.".

Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn.
  • A fresh study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
  • It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A fresh study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a fresh international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

Upcoming Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

Recent findings suggest that the scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

Recent findings suggest that "This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:.

"For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

It has been revealed that determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Sources indicate that stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

According to recent reports, if the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

In a recent development, "In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as vital as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

Sources indicate that the researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

Want your research cited in patents? Publishing open access increases your chances

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paywalled papers are cited less frequently in patents than are open-access studies.Credit: Eoneren/iStock via Getty.
  • In a recent development, open-access science publishing is having an impact far beyond the academic sphere.
  • An analysis of almost 500,000 patents, and the research papers they cite, has shown that open-access papers were cited 1.38 times more often than would be expected on the basis of their prevalence in scientific papers1.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paywalled papers are cited less frequently in patents than are open-access studies.Credit: Eoneren/iStock via Getty.

In a recent development, open-access science publishing is having an impact far beyond the academic sphere. Industries that rely heavily on scientific discoveries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, disproportionately cite open-access work in their patents over paywalled research, a study has found.

An analysis of almost 500,000 patents, and the research papers they cite, has shown that open-access papers were cited 1.38 times more often than would be expected on the basis of their prevalence in scientific papers1.

According to recent reports, when the study authors expanded the definition of open access to include papers available on Sci-Hub, a website that hosts pirated copies of scientific articles, this over-representation was even stronger. Papers that were freely available (either through the journal publishers or Sci-Hub) were 3.41 times more prevalent in patent citations than they were in the wider scientific literature.

In a recent development, the findings, published in Scientometrics, show how heavily inventors lean on open-access research, indicates study co-author Abdelghani Maddi, a scientometrics researcher at Sorbonne University in Paris. When you include platforms such as Sci-Hub, “the numbers are striking”, he says. “Open science is not only about who can read science, it’s about who can build on it.”.

For their analysis, Maddi and his colleagues leveraged the ‘Reliance on Science’ data set, a publicly available tool that identifies citation links between patents and journal publications2. They found that research-intensive industries, such as biotechnology and pharmaceuticals, cite the scientific literature (both open and pay-walled) in their patents much more heavily than do more engineering-based industries, such as vehicle- and construction-equipment manufacturing.

The researchers also showed that patents from countries with a high proportion of high-tech industries, including South Korea, Singapore and Denmark, cite more scientific publications than do those from countries with more heavy manufacturing industries, such as South Africa, Brazil and Italy.

It has been revealed that to track patent citations of open-access papers specifically, the team cross-referenced research publications in the Reliance on Science patent database against those in OpenAlex, an index that catalogues hundreds of millions of scientific documents. They then used a normalization metric to account for differences in open-access publishing practices across research disciplines. Open-access publishing is much more prevalent in the health sciences than it is in computer science, for example, notes Maddi.

Seeing how open-access papers were over-represented in patent citations suggests that making research freely accessible does more than just help people to read and share scientific findings, says study co-author Francesco De Pretis, an applied mathematician at the University of Modena and Reggio Emilia in Italy. It also makes that knowledge more likely to be used in developing newly introduced technologies and inventions, he adds. “Our findings show that open science is not just a matter for academia, it’s also the business of industry and of national economies.”.

Matt Marx, an innovation and entrepreneurship researcher at Cornell University in Ithaca, New York, whose team developed the Reliance on Science database, says the finding that patents tend to cite open-access papers “is especially intriguing”. But he cautions against assuming that ease of access is the only factor at play. “Perhaps inventors are more likely to cite papers they can read because those are open access, or it could be that prominent or key papers are more likely to be open-source,” he says.

Industry observers note that regardless of the exact causes, the access barrier is real, notes Marin Dacos, who heads the open-science taskforce in France’s Ministry of Higher Education, Research and Space. Negotiating contracts with thousands of journal publishers worldwide requires specialist library staff — a resource that is generally only available to large companies and universities, he says.

Manchester City have managed only five clean sheets this season.

Manchester City's leaky defence faces one of its most difficult tasks of the season with a trip to watertight Arsenal, aiming to put right their patchy recent form.

Enzo Maresca's side began the season with eight straight victories but have won only one of their past seven in all competitions inside 90 minutes and head to Emirates Stadium trailing the champions by six points even at this early juncture.

A Premier League defeat on Sunday could well have long-term consequences for City's title aspirations, with Mikel Arteta's men clearly standing above any other top-flight side as the ones to topple.

Though the Gunners dropped points last weekend with a draw at Newcastle, they continue to set the standards with a miserly defence that has conceded only seven goals in the club's opening 11 league games.

Asked why he felt City have dropped off in recent weeks, Maresca - who replaced Pep Guardiola as manager in the summer - said: "For me it's because we've had four months together. Transition requires time.

"It's probably because we won seven games in a row, with Champions League eight in a row. Everyone was thinking at City there's no transition but I've stated many times I am not a magician. There is transition, it's normal.

It has been revealed that "There are eight or nine new players, the manager is new so you need time and you can see different clubs when they had transition how complicated it is. For me, it's completely normal, I'm completely relaxed, no panic at all.".

'Pass, pass, slow, slow' - Man City's slick machine grinding to a halt.

Why Man City can't wear their new kit in Premier League.

"We are conceding too many goals and we need to avoid that," was an obvious statement made by Maresca following last Saturday's 1-1 draw against Fulham.

City followed that up with another home stalemate against Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday and have now conceded in 10 successive games in all competitions for the first time in seven years.

"[It was] far, far too easy to play through [City]," said former England captain Alan Shearer of Rodrigo Muniz's goal for Fulham on Match of the Day.

"Fulham's throw-in was level with their own 18-yard box. For them to get through is not acceptable at any level, let alone when you are playing for Manchester City and Muniz ran past the entire midfield [to score].".

City have managed only five clean sheets all campaign, which is in stark contrast to Arsenal, who have kept double the amount so far, while Newcastle's opening goal ended a run off 445 minutes without the ball hitting their net.

Maresca's men also have an problem by conceding the opener, having done so seven times in the past 10 games, and of the 14 goals they have shipped, six have come inside the first 20 minutes.

An early Arsenal goal may well be an vital factor in deciding Sunday's contest.

Asked how his side can improve defensively, Maresca remarked: "Video [analysis], meetings, [on] pitch coaching, It is a mix of that.

"Some of the goals we concede we can avoid, so hopefully we can do that.".

Man City fan questions what's behind Marc Guehi's recent struggles.

The injury to key defender William Saliba has almost gone unnoticed for Arsenal as Ezri Konsa has stepped in to fill the void at centre-back seamlessly since joining from Aston Villa in the summer.

The England international has established a formidable partnership with Gabriel and the two have quickly formed an impressive understanding this season.

Maresca, meanwhile, admitted he was still "trying to find different" solutions to his team, which has been highlighted by the chopping and changing of his backline.

In 16 Premier League and Champions League games this season, the Italian has used eight different combinations in defence, which has given players little chance of fostering any sort of on-pitch relationships with each other.

City have also made seven errors leading to goals, compared to Arsenal's one.

Industry observers note that "You are concerned in some way because that is a lot of errors leading to goals," stated former City defender Nedum Onuoha. "With some of the best players you ask, 'what are they really good at?' For some it is the fact they don't make mistakes.

"They are ruthless and relentless in the way they play but at this moment in time City are being punished for those errors.

"A manager can have the tactics and do the team talks, but if people are going to continue to make those mistakes, they will suffer.".

The chant of "1-0 to the Arsenal" has been synonymous with the Gunners over the years and it could not be more apt under Arteta.

Since the start of last season, his side have won 16 matches in all competitions by that particular scoreline, compared to six by City.

After beating Sunderland in a chaotic match in September, Maresca stated he would "prefer to win 1-0 than 5-3", suggesting his side needed more control and he re-iterated that message after the Fulham draw.

"Sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference and to keep a clean sheet but in this moment we are not able to do that," he admitted.

City, though, have scored five more league goals than Arsenal in this campaign and Sunday's hosts have injury concerns over goalkeeper David Raya.

The Spaniard is a doubt with the shoulder problem he picked up at Newcastle, and compatriot Kepa Arrizabalaga may deputise again as he did in the 1-1 draw against Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday.

City have fond memories of coming up against Arsenal's stand-in keeper, after Kepa's howler for the opening goal contributed to their 2-0 Carabao Cup final triumph back in March.

A repeat result on Sunday will provide a much-needed morale boost for Maresca and his team.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that MARSHALL, Mich. — Ford Motor has started producing battery cells in the U.S. for its next generation of electric vehicles using technologies licensed by Chinese battery giant CATL.

Industry observers note that the automaker said Wednesday that cell production at a $3 billion plant in Marshall, Michigan — roughly 100 miles west of Detroit — started last month and the cells are now shipping out. They'll be used in prototypes for its Fathom small electric pickup truck, which CEO Jim Farley has touted as rivaling Tesla and Chinese competitors.

Recent findings suggest that the production marks a milestone for the Detroit automaker and is the next step toward using lower-cost lithium iron phosphate, or LFP, battery cells in U.S. vehicles. The technology was created in the U.S. but commercialized largely in China.

It has been revealed that the automaker's decision to make the batteries at the roughly 2 million-square-foot facility has been criticized by some lawmakers and U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over Ford's ties to CATL.

It has been revealed that alan Clarke, Ford's vice president of advanced development projects, said licensing the technology from CATL helped the automaker bring the low-cost battery chemistry to the U.S. as promptly as possible.

"If we want to get to being able to produce affordable EVs in the United States, we need to also do it the fastest way possible," Clarke said Tuesday during a tour of the facility. "CATL being the biggest in the world means that they're the best supplier to get us that technology and help us learn ourselves how to produce LFP cells.".

The U.S. government has increased scrutiny of Chinese ties with U.S. companies even as President Donald Trump is meeting this week with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

It has been revealed that in September, Duffy sent a letter to Farley expressing "profound concern" about Ford's ties to Chinese companies that it believes could be detrimental to the Detroit carmaker and the U.S. automotive industry. The White House a day later followed up by commending the automaker for its domestic jobs and manufacturing.

Ford — the largest producer of U.S. vehicles — has routinely touted its American roots, jobs and manufacturing, especially as the Biden and Trump administrations have pushed to onshore and grow U.S. production.

It has been revealed that ford's battery plant in Marshall is expected to be capable of producing 40 battery cells a minute, equating to 20 gigawatt-hours annually for EVs and the tech giant's energy storage business. That's down from initial plans of up to 40 gigawatt-hours annually amid an EV pullback by the automaker and broader industry.

Ford has noted the production pace will help reduce battery costs and that the facility has room for additional capacity if needed.

The facility is highly automated, but Ford said it's still in the early stages of certifying its processes, as it prepares to ramp up cell production next year before the expected launch of the Fathom pickup during the fourth quarter of 2027.

Tech Report: Bizarre deep-sea fish with a see-through head captured in stunning 4K

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1046 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard.
  • Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

Recent findings suggest that "Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," noted Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.].

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean.

It has been revealed that the discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

To investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt.

The barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

In a recent development, the clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details.

According to recent reports, scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

Sources indicate that the team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

Recent findings suggest that "Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," mentioned Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.".

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives.

The rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

According to recent reports, MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the new flagship research vessel David Packard.

MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

A Latest Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.
  • Industry observers note that to rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build upcoming data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia.
  • An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German firm Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a upcoming breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.

Industry observers note that to rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build upcoming data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy—like Scandinavia. But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components, and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.

An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German firm Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a upcoming breed of chip—photonic processors—meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.

Whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.

The aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.

Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud tech giant IONOS as part of a pilot program. It claims that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.

Earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a newly introduced class of hardware.

This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

According to recent reports, WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?

Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.

If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a latest processor that takes care of the heavy math.

Sources indicate that the cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.

It has been revealed that how would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?

According to recent reports, light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function. [The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.

Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.

What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?

The Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.

Industry observers note that linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.

We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.

What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?

I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.

Recent findings suggest that under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.

Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?

Recent findings suggest that there’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.

But if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.

It’s a chicken and egg problem, right? Until developers are building models to run on this type of processor, it’s going to be difficult to sell them to cloud providers. Equally, until photonic processors are available for people to use, it’s going to be tough to convince developers to design for them.

Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology, it will need time to get the credibility and trust that’s needed for a organization like Google to build data center infrastructure around it.

That’s the reason we chose to go into data centers with proof of concept systems, to validate that photonic computing is robust enough to withstand that environment.

We want to invite the world to compute on our systems. We are building a new chicken, so you can start producing eggs. Let’s find out together whether they’re tasty or not.

What else should I understand about why photonic processors are not already widely in use?

If hypothetically we received an order of 100,000 [photonic processors], we at Q.ANT are ready, but I’m not sure about the suppliers.

It has been revealed that hardware is not software. On the assembly side, it will need [time] before we have the same robust supply chain as the semiconductor world.

Do you expect to suffer from the same problem as other hardware challengers in securing capacity with the big chip manufacturers?

Industry observers note that [To produce Q.ANT chips] you only need 90 nanometer node technology, from the 2000s. A lot of foundries already use this capability to produce chips that are super cheap. With this technology, you can use the same line to produce high-performance chips with a much higher street price, without massive upfront investment in your assets.

That resonates well with the industry.

Are Q.ANT processors built to function alongside a particular brand of GPUs—say, Nvidia or AMD—or are they totally agnostic?

There’s no need to go single-sided with a particular GPU. We want to have the freedom to cooperate with any of them.

Either way, we are not competitive to GPUs, we complete their function set.

Can you imagine a future in which AI models run entirely on photonic processors, or will they always be a sidekick?

If we see an opportunity in five years to attack the GPU as well, we would not be shy about taking it. But at the same time, I do not know what workloads in five years are going to be like.

It depends on the architecture of future AI models, you mean?

Could the chance to perform certain calculations more cheaply with photonic processors change the way that AI engineers design future models?

The core message is that we need to do something to fight the energy cost in the AI stack.

That’s where we see the future of AI: very data-optimized models that allow for tasks of the same quality, but at a fraction of the energy—and therefore a fraction of the operating cost.
