#150855. Breaking: Is free will an illusion? Latest brain research reveals a surprising twist

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (866 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Is free will an illusion? Latest brain research reveals a surprising twist

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine you’re in line at your favorite bakery, deciding whether to have a doughnut or a tart.
  • Industry observers note that by the time you’re at the front of the line, however, only tarts are left.
  • Recent findings suggest that these two decisions feel completely different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine you’re in line at your favorite bakery, deciding whether to have a doughnut or a tart. You weigh them up, the doughnut wins, and you settle on that.

Industry observers note that by the time you’re at the front of the line, however, only tarts are left. So, you buy one.

Recent findings suggest that these two decisions feel completely different. One involves deliberation based on our unique and personal preferences, while the other involves simply recognizing and picking the only available option.

But our latest research published in the journal Imaging Neuroscience shows our brains actually make these decisions in surprisingly similar ways.

When we make free decisions, we recognize multiple options exist, weigh them up, and commit to one based on something internal: our preferences, values and goals.

Forced decisions are different. There’s only one possible outcome, and our job is simply to identify the option and take it.

Industry observers note that because free decisions feel so closely tied to who we are, neuroscientists have long assumed they rely on different processes in the brain compared to forced decisions. Some brain imaging studies support this, showing different patterns of neural activity distributed across the brain.

However, knowing where in the brain free choices happen tells us little about how they are formed – and whether this process is any different from forced decisions.

Decades of research have shown that, to make decisions, our brains gradually gather evidence for each option over time.

Industry observers note that think of it like a judge evaluating the facts of a case. Once enough evidence has been accumulated in favour of one party, a verdict is reached. For some types of decisions, this happens very rapidly (over hundreds of milliseconds), making it feel like the choice just popped into your head.

By measuring electrical brain activity, researchers have identified a brain signal that reflects this accumulation of evidence during simple decisions – such as judging whether a traffic light is red or green.

According to recent reports, like a loading bar building to 100%, the signal gradually rises to a particular level before a decision is made. Because the action of neurons in the brain is noisy, this decision-making process also occurs in a noisy fashion: rather than climbing steadily towards one option, the signal fluctuates back and forth between the alternatives.

This partly explains why we aren’t always consistent with our choices – even when our preferences are stable, some days we will go for the tart and others, the doughnut.

It has been revealed that this signal has been identified for forced decisions with a clear correct answer. But what about choices that are open-ended – shaped not just by what’s in front of us, but by something internal like preferences or personal goals?

To answer this question, we recorded people’s brain activity while they chose between sets of colored balloons. They viewed either two balloons of different colors to freely choose between, or a single balloon they were forced to pick.

They pressed a button the moment they made their choice, and we tracked how brain activity unfolded in the lead-up to that moment.

Recent findings suggest that for both free and forced decisions, the brain activity unfolded in a very similar way. Like a loading bar, it climbed steadily to the same peak level just before a choice was made. When people decided swiftly, the signal increased faster. When they took longer, it rose more slowly.

That’s exactly what you would expect if the brain were tracking and weighing up evidence over time, rather than simply reacting to a decision at the last moment.

From this finding, one might assume the brain forms free and forced decisions in the same way, suggesting decision-making in the brain may be more automatic than it feels.

This echoes famous experiments by neuroscientist Benjamin Libet in the 1980s. He and colleagues found brain activity begins ramping up before people are even consciously aware of their intention to act – suggesting the brain has already begun deciding before the person consciously realizes they’ve made a choice.

But while the process may be automatic, what the brain is accumulating tells a different story. The evidence it weighs up is drawn entirely from who you are – your preferences, your goals, your experiences. Two people may go through the same neural process and land on the same choice, and yet arrive there for completely different reasons.

Industry observers note that so rather than asking whether our choices are truly free, perhaps the better question is what it really means for a choice to be yours. And the next time you find yourself in line at the bakery, know that your brain has already been quietly gathering evidence toward your baked good of choice, and that choice happens a little faster than you realize.

On this day in space! Nov. 26, 2011: NASA's 2-ton nuclear-powered Curiosity rover rolls out to Mars

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars.
  • Industry observers note that the Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet.
  • According to recent reports, it introduced on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars.

Industry observers note that the Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars, or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past.

According to recent reports, it introduced on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a upcoming landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface.

It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet.

Curiosity was the largest rover ever launched to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success.

After its smooth landing, Curiosity lived up to its original name: the Mars Science Laboratory. Within weeks, Curiosity fulfilled its primary mission. It found evidence of ancient running water on Mars. It later found organic molecules on Mars as well.

Curiosity's primary mission was expected to last just about one Martian year (687 Earth days, or about two Earth years), as the rover explored its Gale Crater landing site. But NASA has extended the mission as the rover continues to operate in good health.

In fact, Curiosity has survived long enough to welcome its successor to Mars, the Perseverance rover, which landed in February 2021 on a mission to collect the first samples for later retrieval. Perseverance used the same basic 2-ton design, plutonium power system and sky crane landing system to reach Mars.

And today, a ground-based twin of the Curiosity rover, called Promise, is being outfitted for an upcoming mission to the moon.

#150850. Industry News: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

Industry News: This 6-million-year-old whale may have had the most crooked face in mammal history

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A bizarre prehistoric whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so crooked that researchers initially suspected its fossilized skull had been distorted after death.
  • According to recent reports, sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are already known for having some of the strangest head shapes among mammals.
  • Now, an international team of scientists has identified an extinct pygmy sperm whale species that took this unusual anatomy to an entirely new level.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A bizarre prehistoric whale that lived roughly 6 million years ago had a face so crooked that researchers initially suspected its fossilized skull had been distorted after death. Instead, its extraordinary shape was completely natural and may represent the most extreme facial asymmetry ever documented in a mammal.

According to recent reports, sperm whales and pygmy sperm whales are already known for having some of the strangest head shapes among mammals. While most vertebrates have bodies and skulls that are roughly symmetrical on both sides, toothed whales have evolved uneven skull structures to accommodate specialized organs responsible for producing sound and navigating through echolocation.

Now, an international team of scientists has identified an extinct pygmy sperm whale species that took this unusual anatomy to an entirely new level. Named Scaphokogia huachafo, the whale lived during the Late Miocene, between 6.3 and 5.6 million years ago, and measured approximately 2.7 meters in length. Its fossilized skull displays the most extreme facial asymmetry known in any whale or dolphin, and possibly in any mammal.

A Prehistoric Whale With an Extraordinary Skull.

"Cranial asymmetry in toothed whales is directly linked to the development of fatty structures in the forehead that are involved in sound production. But in Scaphokogia huachafo, this asymmetry went far beyond the area around the blowhole. Both bony nostrils are shifted entirely to the left side of the skull, while the facial bones differ dramatically in size and position. The skull looks completely crooked," explains Aldo Benites-Palomino, lead author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that benites-Palomino investigated the fossil during his doctoral research at the University of Zurich's Department of Paleontology. He is currently an assistant professor at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU).

The whale's extraordinary appearance also inspired its scientific name. The word huachafo comes from Peruvian Spanish and is commonly used to describe something excessively flashy, bizarre, extravagant, or even tacky.

"In Peru, huachafo is an everyday word for anything that is flashy, over-the-top, bizarre, extravagant or difficult to categorize aesthetically," states Benites-Palomino.

Sources indicate that "When we looked at the proportions of this whale - with its face strongly shifted to the left and its oversized, downward-curving snout - it broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans. Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it.".

Scientists Initially Suspected the Skull Was Deformed.

In a recent development, the remarkable fossil was originally recovered during the mid-1990s from the Pisco Formation in southern Peru. This desert region is famous among paleontologists for its exceptionally preserved fossils of ancient marine animals.

According to recent reports, benites-Palomino first encountered the specimen in 2015 while preparing his Bachelor's thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima. Its dramatically uneven shape immediately raised an crucial question: Was the skull genuinely this crooked when the whale was alive, or had millions of years of geological pressure distorted it?

"The initial suspicion with skulls this distorted is always taphonomy - that the specimen may have been flattened or twisted by sediment pressure over millions of years," says Benites-Palomino.

"But the sutures are fully closed, and there are no fractures, pathologies or deformations elsewhere on the skull. This was genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.".

The findings confirmed that the extraordinary asymmetry was part of the whale's natural anatomy, rather than damage caused by burial, fossilization, or disease.

A Bizarre Adaptation for Hunting Along the Seafloor.

The whale's unusual skull also offers clues about how it survived. Modern sperm whales typically pursue squid in deep ocean waters, but Scaphokogia huachafo appears to have followed a very different hunting strategy. Its anatomy suggests that it was highly adapted to searching for food along the bottom of shallow coastal waters.

It has been revealed that one of its most distinctive features was a large, tube-shaped snout strengthened by dense bone and cartilage that had hardened into bone. These heavy structures served as natural ballast, moving the whale's center of gravity forward and downward.

Its snout also pointed downward at an angle of 31 degrees relative to the rest of its skull. By reconstructing the joint connecting the skull to the first neck vertebra, known as the atlas, scientists determined that Scaphokogia could bend its head downward by as much as 55 degrees.

"The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom," explains Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, co-author of the study and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich.

"The combination of dense bone, the downward-curving snout and the flexible neck articulation allowed the animal to move directly above the seabed and feed close to the sediment.".

Researchers also believe the whale may have relied on its highly specialized echolocation system to locate prey beneath the soft sediment of coastal environments. Unlike other marine mammals that forage along the ocean floor, Scaphokogia lacked the sensitive facial whiskers or specialized visual adaptations that can help animals find food near the bottom.

Instead, its extraordinarily asymmetrical skull may have supported a sophisticated biological sonar system that allowed it to detect hidden prey.

Sources indicate that this unusual feeding strategy represents a specialized way of life that no longer exists among modern marine mammals. As ocean conditions shifted toward the end of the Miocene, the ecological niche occupied by Scaphokogia disappeared, eventually giving way to the marine mammal communities familiar today.

The discovery provides a remarkable glimpse into how far evolution once pushed the anatomy of whales, producing a creature whose dramatically crooked face was not a deformity, but an adaptation to a vanished underwater world.

Billy Ray Cyrus is celebrating in the heart of family.

The Hannah Montana alum also reserved some special words for his now son-in-law.

"Growing up in Australia, my love of music was predominant over everything," Firerose told People. "I've known his music since forever.".

What started as a friendship turned into more during the darkest days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

"This has been absolutely the most crazy insane scam I have ever heard of," Billy Ray mentioned in a statement to E! News. "Let alone the fact I'm right in the center and basically the target of the scheme. It's unfortunate it played out this way.".

Trace's Public Plea to Dad Billy Ray.

Reunited and Miley Breaks Silence.

Michael Noetzel, the upcoming justice minister in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, has come under fire for a now-deleted social media post promoting the far-left antifa.

The controversy centers on a photo of Noetzel wearing a T-shirt with the historic 1932 antifa logo and raising his left fist.

Noetzel, a representative of the socialist Left Party, also wrote that it is important for young people to attend antifa meetings.

Philipp Amthor, who serves as acting head of the state chapter of the conservative CDU, demanded that Noetzel "make an unambiguous statement now regarding his position on left-wing extremist and violence-prone groups within the antifa scene.".

Enrico Schult, who is a parliamentary group leader of the far-right populist AfD, stated: "If you have such a hard time distancing yourself from violent structures, then you are unfit to serve as minister of justice.".

The ministry stated that Noetzel "naturally takes a clear stand against extremism.".

The ministry also identified right-wing extremism as the greatest threat to democracy and that combating it is a priority.

The German government looks to acquire a stake in the Canada-based artificial intelligence technology firm Cohere for the symbolic sum of €1.

The Digital Ministry confirmed media reports that the Finance Ministry had approved the government's small stake in the multinational firm.

According to a ministry spokesperson, the government is presently considering investing a larger sum.

Cohere would commit itself "to helping increase competitiveness in AI in Germany and to securing jobs, research and development and investment in Germany," the spokesperson said.

He added that the German government would receive "specific governance guarantees that safeguard the goal of digital sovereignty.".

Cohere's goal is to develop sovereign AI services for the public administration, as well as finance, defense, energy, telecommunications, and healthcare.

This technology is designed to operate independently of major US data center operators.

The ban comes amid a settlement between Freigang, 28, who is also the captain of Frankfurt Eintracht, and the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA).

Freigang has been the subject of proceedings for several months, having been accused of not being at the location she specified for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026.

That amount will, however, by offset by the €360,000 that the Catholic Church's Independent Commission for Recognition Payments has already paid to the claimant.

The woman had previously had her claim rejected by the Cologne Regional Court, which, although it accepted that the victim had been severely sexually abused by a priest in the 1970s and 1980s, argued that the archdiocese could not be made responsible for the crimes because the man had acted "more or less as a private individual.".

The higher regional court has now overturned that ruling at an appeal, saying that the priest had approached the claimant "under the cover of his church work" when he was a deacon.

It said he used his standing in the church to be allowed to take in foster children, of whom the claimant was one.

The priest was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2022.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has called for closer economic and political partnerships with African countries as he wound up what was probably his last trip to the continent as head of state.

Speaking in Kenya, Steinmeier said that there were great variations in the state of development between individual countries and even within some of them.

"But I believe it is worthwhile investing in Africa and in relations with African countries," he said.

Recent findings suggest that he said this was not just meant with a view to possible investment by German companies drawn by Africa's mostly young national populations and developing markets. Chocolate manufacturers in Germany produced less in 2025 than the year before.

According to figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) released on Thursday, around 1 million metric tons (1.1 US tons) of chocolate products containing cocoa were made in Germany in 2025, compared with 1.1 million tons in 2024.

This represents a reduction of 5.7%.

Much of the chocolate produced in Germany is exported (916,200 tons in 2025), while considerable amounts are also imported (530,000 tons in 2025), with a quarter of that amount coming from neighboring Belgium.

Altogether 13.4% of exports went to France, followed by Poland (9.6%) and the UK (9.3%).

According to the survey of 9,000 members, more than 70% feel that the situation for police on the evening would improve if such a ban were in place.

Altogether 54% of respondents who had been on duty during the past 10 years of Latest Year's Eve festivities reported having been in a dangerous or threatening situation caused by fireworks.

A whole 195 respondents said they had been injured by fireworks on the evening.

The group includes 86 organizations, among them Environmental Action Germany (DUH) and the GdP, who have called for a ban on private fireworks to protect people, emergency personnel, animals and the environment.

Plans foreseeing a rise of €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in the budget for the Interior Ministry have been approved by the three parties in Germany's coalition government, after much debate centering on something that makes up a relatively small proportion of that money: the controversial planned centers for rejected asylum seekers in Rwanda.

According to Klaus-Peter Willsch of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), just €5 million are earmarked for the so-called return hubs, shared between several European countries.

He said the €20 million that has often been cited as being for the Rwanda migration centers was not only for the hubs in that country, but for other potential projects in third countries as well.

Despite the relatively small amounts of money involved, the Rwanda plans devised by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) along with Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece came under fire not only from coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) but particularly from opposition parties.

The Green Party and the Left Party both rejected the idea for ethical reasons, with Green lawmaker Leon Eckert speaking of "state-organized human trafficking," while Dietmar Bartsch of the Left pointed out that the deal was being made with an authoritarian regime.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), for its part, mentioned it found the intends too soft, with parliamentarian Marcus Bühl calling them a "smoke screen," as just 20 rejected asylum-seekers from Germany were to be initially sent to Rwanda under the scheme.

The Bundestag is conducting its concluding debates on the budget for 2027 ahead of a final vote scheduled for Friday.

On Thursday, the focus will initially be on the individual budget for the Interior Ministry led by Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

The government foresees that the ministry, which is responsible for the federal police and the domestic intelligence agency BfV, among other things, will receive some €16.8 billion in 2027 ($18.43 billion), around €1 billion more than this year.

Lawmakers will then go on to debate the individual budgets for the Economics and Energy Ministry, the Ministry for Housing, Urban Development and Building, the Ministry of Food and Agriculture and the Ministry for Education, Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth.

Opening the debates on Wednesday, Merz described the tight budget as an "accurate reflection" of the "difficult situation as a country — geopolitically, technologically, and demographically" — that Germany finds itself in.

"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know.

As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky.

Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane.

Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky. Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below.

This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you promptly find a steady view of the moon. For a closer look at craters and the terminator, make sure to grab a 9mm or 12mm eyepiece and get stronger magnification.

Recent findings suggest that the bright star Spica will glow less than five degrees away from Venus before dawn on Nov. 27 — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length against the night sky.

In a recent development, spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. However, the system still makes for a dazzling target, appearing as a magnificent blue-white star when viewed through the eyepiece of a 4-inch telescope.

Check that the sun is safely below the horizon before turning your telescope on Venus to observe a crescent of light playing across the planet's dense atmosphere. Over the coming weeks and months, Venus will appear increasingly illuminated as it moves farther away from Earth in its orbit, while its apparent size through a telescope will gradually decrease.

Want to get a closer look at the planets of the solar system and the stars beyond? Then be sure to check out our roundups of the best telescopes and smart telescopes for observing the night sky.

Tech Report: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A century after the Taung Child transformed our understanding of where humans came from, scientists are discovering that this famous fossil still has surprises to reveal.
  • The international study was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB).
  • First discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child provided the first concrete evidence supporting the African origins of humanity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A century after the Taung Child transformed our understanding of where humans came from, scientists are discovering that this famous fossil still has surprises to reveal. A upcoming study published in Nature dates the ancient remains to between 2.96 and 3.03 million years ago and suggests that the human family tree in southern Africa was much more complicated than previously believed.

The international study was led by Professor Gabriele Macho of the Archaeology, Environmental Changes and Geo-Chemistry (AMGC) research group at Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB). The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how early human relatives evolved and how different species were related.

First discovered in South Africa in 1924, the Taung Child provided the first concrete evidence supporting the African origins of humanity. It also became the original "type specimen" used to define the species Australopithecus africanus. However, scientists never established definitive criteria for assigning later fossil discoveries to this species. As a result, the Taung Child remains the only fossil that can be identified with certainty as Australopithecus africanus.

"For over 100 years, we assumed the Taung Child was just one of many similar fossils from the era," indicates Professor Gabriele Macho. "Our findings turn that on its head. The human family tree wasn't a neat, straight trunk -- it was a chaotic, tangled bush driven by climate shifts.".

Ancient Fossils Reveal a More Complex Human Family Tree.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate how the Taung Child compared with other early human relatives, researchers examined tooth structure and patterns of brain and dental development during growth. They found that several adult fossils traditionally classified as Australopithecus africanus followed developmental patterns that differed from those of the Taung Child.

Industry observers note that differences in brain development were particularly revealing. They suggest that fossils previously grouped into a single species may actually represent several distinct hominin species that inhabited the Sterkfontein region, either at the same time or during different periods.

These findings raise notable questions about the diversity of our ancient ancestors and suggest that early human evolution followed a much more complicated path than scientists once assumed.

How Climate Change Shaped Human Evolution.

According to recent reports, the researchers believe that dramatic environmental changes played a major role in creating this evolutionary diversity. Millions of years ago, southern Africa experienced repeated shifts between wetter and drier climates, continually transforming the landscape and the habitats available to early human relatives.

According to recent reports, as suitable environments expanded and contracted, ancient hominin populations moved with them. Some groups became geographically isolated and evolved along different paths, while others eventually came back into contact and interbred. These changing conditions also exposed populations to different predators and pathogens, creating additional pressures that shaped their evolution.

Southern Africa's position along the boundary between tropical and temperate ecosystems made it especially important in this process. Over thousands of years, shifting habitats may have repeatedly brought different hominin species together, creating opportunities for interbreeding and hybridization.

A Greener South Africa 3 Million Years Ago.

The study also reveals a surprising picture of the environment in which the Taung Child lived. Evidence preserved in fossilized pollen indicates that the region was once considerably wetter and more heavily forested than it is today.

Researchers identified evidence of tree species that are now found hundreds of kilometers to the northeast, suggesting that the landscape surrounding the Taung Child was dramatically different from modern South Africa.

Together, these discoveries challenge the traditional view of human evolution as a relatively straightforward progression from one species to another. Instead, they point to a shifting network of populations that repeatedly separated, adapted, reunited, and sometimes interbred as environmental conditions changed.

Recent findings suggest that more than 100 years after its discovery, the Taung Child is once again transforming our understanding of human origins. Its latest secrets suggest that the emergence of our own genus, Homo, was preceded by a far more diverse and interconnected world of ancient human relatives than previously recognized.

Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.

Walmart said global e-commerce sales surged 17% in the fiscal third quarter, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.

In a recent development, walmart remarked it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.

CEO John Furner told CNBC's Becky Quick that the organization has seen higher-than-expected diesel costs, but that tariff refunds have helped the retailer to offset those inputs and maintain lower prices.

"The reality is that increases in diesel fuel and transportation, they do work their way into cost of goods," Furner stated in an exclusive interview. "So we're hoping to see these costs come down as soon as possible, and we'll keep prices as low as we can.".

CFO John David Rainey told CNBC that growth in online orders for Walmart and Sam's Club was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and reduced prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.

Recent findings suggest that "This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses.".

Industry observers note that walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to increase between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared with previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey stated Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.

Sources indicate that walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.

Here's how the firm performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

Industry observers note that for the quarter ended Oct. 31, the organization reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, a year earlier. Revenue rose 5.2%.

Adjusting for investment gains and losses, tax matters and reorganization charges, Walmart earned 65 cents per share.

Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from a year earlier. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.

Furner also remarked Walmart is seeing encouraging adoption of its artificial intelligence agent, named Sparky, especially ahead of the holiday season. He said it's led to customer basket increases of 40% on average.

"It just is a great way of just completing the entire basket and solving entire the solution for people," he mentioned.

Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.

Recent findings suggest that in October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Walmart+ and Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer stand-alone memberships, as well.

Recent findings suggest that furner told CNBC the upcoming membership has brought roughly 2 million new people into Sam's Club since its launch in late October. Though the organization reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey added that it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more.".

The company on Thursday noted its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer is typically well insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter, the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.

Rainey noted Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start.".

In a recent development, the massive-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.

Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year to date.

Scientists tested 212 plant-based foods. Every single one contained fungal toxins

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1066 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a latest study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.
  • Researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes.
  • Mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every one of 212 plant-based foods and drinks tested in a latest study contained at least one naturally occurring fungal toxin, raising questions about the potential health effects of regularly consuming these products.

Researchers examined a wide selection of vegetarian and vegan products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives and dairy substitutes. They detected at least one of 19 mycotoxins in every product, and many contained multiple toxins.

Mycotoxins are poisonous substances produced by certain fungi, including molds. They can enter the food supply when agricultural crops become contaminated during growing, harvesting, or storage.

In a recent development, the investigation was led by scientists at the University of Parma in Italy, with contributions from Cranfield University. The researchers analyzed 212 products, including plant-based meat alternatives (PMBAs) and plant-based beverages (PBBs). The selection covered foods commonly found on supermarket shelves, such as vegan burgers, vegetarian chicken pieces, vegan sausages, and oat, almond, and soy milk.

Although the findings highlight how widespread these naturally occurring contaminants can be, the researchers also identified an important reassuring detail. Every product contained mycotoxin concentrations below recommended European Union guideline levels, which the team said reflected the high food quality standards maintained by the UK food industry.

Why Plant-Based Foods Can Contain Fungal Toxins.

Many of the ingredients used to manufacture plant-based foods are particularly susceptible to fungal contamination. Grains, legumes, and seeds can encounter mold in fields or storage facilities, creating opportunities for mycotoxins to develop before the ingredients reach food manufacturers.

In a recent development, unlike bacteria or viruses, mycotoxins are chemical substances produced by certain fungi. Their presence in food does not necessarily mean the product contains living mold, and detecting a toxin does not automatically mean the food is unsafe. The potential health risk depends on factors such as the type of toxin, its concentration, and how much a person consumes over time.

Recent findings suggest that this distinction is especially vital for people who eat plant-based products frequently. Someone whose diet regularly includes meat substitutes, dairy alternatives, grains, and legumes may encounter these substances through several different foods rather than a single source.

Could Repeated Exposure Pose Health Risks?

While the concentrations detected in the UK products were below recommended EU guidelines, researchers say the potential effects of repeated exposure deserve closer attention.

Earlier studies have suggested that consuming small amounts of mycotoxins regularly may contribute to cumulative exposure and potentially increase health risks. In other words, assessing a single product may not provide a complete picture of a person's overall dietary exposure.

Eating one of these products occasionally is unlikely to cause problems based on the levels reported. However, a diet that relies heavily or exclusively on plant-based foods could involve repeated exposure to mycotoxins from numerous ingredients and products. Researchers say understanding the combined effects is important for evaluating possible long-term health consequences.

The severity of mycotoxin exposure varies depending on the compounds involved and the amount consumed. At sufficiently high or harmful exposure levels, certain mycotoxins can damage the liver and kidneys, interfere with normal immune system function, and increase the risk of cancer.

Recent findings suggest that the latest findings do not establish that the tested products cause these conditions. Instead, they provide information that scientists can use to estimate how much exposure consumers may receive through their diets and develop more accurate food safety risk assessments for the UK population.

Scientists Call for Better Monitoring of Plant-Based Ingredients.

According to recent reports, andrea Patriarca, Senior Lecturer in Mycology at Cranfield University, emphasized that mycotoxins are a natural part of the food environment and should not discourage people from eating a varied diet. Mycology is the branch of biology devoted to studying fungi, including molds and yeasts.

Sources indicate that "Mycotoxins occur naturally in foods and cannot be completely avoided. As consumers, we should not be frightened or deterred from enjoying a variety of products.

It has been revealed that however, a significant concern arises when newly introduced foods enter the market, as there are currently no established regulations to monitor mycotoxins. We collaborate closely with various sectors in the food industry, from farmers to food companies, to help implement effective mycotoxin management integrated within food safety standards. The data from our research helps food safety organizations in assessing risks, particularly in complex multi-ingredient products.

We are at the moment collaborating with the University of Parma to evaluate the risks faced by the population based on different dietary habits. Our aim is to advise policymakers and raise awareness among vulnerable consumers.".

The researchers are particularly interested in how food safety monitoring can keep pace with the growing range of plant-based products. Foods made from multiple ingredients present additional challenges because each component may introduce different contaminants, making overall exposure more difficult to assess.

Industry observers note that their work also underscores the importance of monitoring raw materials throughout the food production process. Identifying and controlling contamination before ingredients are combined into finished products could help manufacturers manage potential risks more effectively.

What the Findings Mean for Plant-Based Diets.

The discovery of fungal toxins in all 212 products highlights the importance of studying dietary exposure across multiple foods, rather than evaluating each product in isolation.

For consumers, the results are not a reason to abandon vegan or vegetarian foods. The concentrations measured were below recommended EU guidelines, and the researchers stress that mycotoxins cannot be completely eliminated from the food supply.

Industry observers note that instead, the study points to the need for continued research into how different eating habits influence exposure, particularly among people who depend heavily on plant-based products. The University of Parma and Cranfield University are continuing their collaboration to investigate these dietary patterns, identify potentially vulnerable groups, and provide evidence that can inform future food safety policies.

The research, titled "Mycotoxin contamination in plant-based beverages and meat alternatives: A survey of the UK market," was published in the journal Food Control.

The study was conducted as part of the European Union-funded Horizon Europe FunShield4Med project (HORIZON-WIDERA-2021-ACCESS-03), Grant Agreement No 101079173.

  • Recent findings suggest that “We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turkey’s persecuted pro-Kurdish party has emerged as a kingmaker in the country’s upcoming election, playing a decisive role that may just tip the balance enough to unseat two-decade ruler Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

In a key setback to the Turkish president and leader of the Justice and Development Party (AK Party), the pro-Kurdish Peoples’ Democratic Party (HDP) last month confirmed that it would not put forward its own presidential candidate, a move analysts say allows its supporters to vote for Erdogan’s main rival.

Recent findings suggest that “We are facing a turning point that will shape the future of Turkey and (its) society,” said the HDP in a statement on March 23. “To fulfill our historical responsibility against the one-man rule, we will not field a presidential candidate in (the) May 14 elections.”.

In a recent development, it is a twist of irony for the Turkish strongman, who spent the better half of the past decade cracking down on the party after it began chipping away at his voter base. Its former leader Selahattin Demirtas has been in prison for nearly seven years and the party faces possible closure by a court for suspected collusion with the militant Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK) and affiliated groups. But its influence may nonetheless determine the course of Turkey’s politics.

The HDP’s decision not to field a candidate came just three days after head of the Republican People’s Party (CHP) Kemal Kilicdaroglu, Erdogan’s main rival, visited the party’s co-chairs. He told reporters that the solution to Turkey’s problems, “including the Kurdish problem” lies in parliament,” according to Turkish media.

Kilicdaroglu, who represents the six-party Nation Alliance opposition bloc, is the strongest contender to run against Erdogan in years. And while the HDP hasn’t yet declared whether it will put its weight behind him, analysts say it is the kingmaker in the elections.

Erdogan's 'polar opposite' wants to replace him as president of Turkey.

It has been revealed that “It was a carefully crafted political discourse,” Hisyar Ozsoy, deputy co-chair of the HDP and a member of parliament from the predominantly Kurdish province of Diyarbakir, told CNN. “We are not going to have our own candidate, and we will leave it to the international community to interpret it the way they wish.”.

Experts say the crackdown on the HDP is rooted in the threat it poses to Erdogan politically, as well as its position as one of the main parties representing Turkey’s Kurds, an ethnic minority from which a separatist militant movement has emerged.

It has been revealed that the party and the Kurdish people have had a complicated relationship with Erdogan. The leader courted the Kurds in earlier years by granting them more rights and reversing restrictions on the use of their language. Relations with the HDP were also cordial once, as Erdogan worked with the party on a brief peace process with the PKK.

But ties between Erdogan and the HDP later turned sour, and the HDP fell under a sweeping crackdown aimed at the PKK and their affiliates.

Kurds are the biggest minority in Turkey, making up between 15% and 20% of the population, according to Minority Rights Group International.

It is unclear if the HDP will endorse Kilicdaroglu, but analysts say that the deliberate distance may be beneficial for the opposition candidate.

Sources indicate that the accusations against the HDP place it in a precarious position during the elections. It right now faces a case in Turkey’s Constitutional Court over suspected ties to the PKK, which is designated as a terrorist group by Turkey, the United States and the European Union. Knowing it may be banned at any moment, its candidates are running under the Green Left Party in parliament.

If the opposition is seen as allying with the HDP, Erdogan’s AK Party may use its influence in the media to discredit it as being pro-PKK, stated Murat Somer, a political science professor at Koc University in Istanbul and author of Return to Point Zero, a book on the Turkish-Kurdish question in Turkey.

The HDP’s threat to Erdogan’s hold on power became apparent after the June 2015 election, the first general election it participated in. It won 13% of the seats, denying the ruling AK Party its majority for the first time since 2002. Erdogan, however, called a snap election five months later, which led to a drop in the HDP’s support to 10.7%, as well as the restoration of the AK Party’s overall majority.

Sources indicate that “They are a kingmaker in these elections because the HDP gets about half of the votes of the Kurdish population in Turkey,” said Somer, adding that the other, more conservative Kurdish voters have traditionally voted for Erdogan’s AK Party. And last month, the Free Cause Party (HUDA-PAR), a tiny Kurdish-Islamist party announced support for Erdogan in the elections. The party has never won seats in parliament.

Erdogan's political fate may rest on his response to the earthquake.

The HDP knows that its position is key to the outcome of next month’s vote, but that it’s also in a delicate situation.

“We want to play the game wisely, and we need to be very careful,” mentioned Ozsoy, adding that the party wants to avoid a “contaminated political climate” where the elections are polarized “between a very ugly ultra-nationalist discourse against Kilicdaroglu and others.”.

The party was founded in 2012 with a number of aims, said Ozsoy, one of which was “peaceful and democratic resolution of the Kurdish conflict.”.

Somer mentioned that the party was seen to be “an initiative” of the PKK, which later led to a heavy government crackdown on it in the name of counterterrorism.

Its former leader Demirtas remains an influential figure.

The Turkish government has been trying to link the HDP to the PKK but has so far failed to prove “a real connection,” remarked Asli Aydintasbas, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington, DC.

A post-Erdogan Turkey may give some breathing space to the Kurds and Kurdish-dominated parties in Turkey, Aydintasbas told CNN, noting that many Kurdish voters have recently left Erdogan’s camp. “For HDP, this is more than just an ideological choice,” she remarked. “It’s a matter of survival.”.

Ozsoy states his party understands what’s at stake, not only for Turkey’s Kurds but for all its minorities.

Industry observers note that “We are aware of our responsibility here. We are aware of our role. We know we are in a kingmaker position,” the HDP lawmaker said.

#150835. Industry News: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

Industry News: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A fresh approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments.
  • In experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass.
  • The findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising fresh direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A fresh approach to weight loss could help the body burn more fat while preserving muscle, potentially overcoming one of the major drawbacks of existing obesity treatments. Researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have identified a compound that increases the amount of energy the body uses rather than simply reducing how much food a person eats.

In experiments with mice, the compound improved blood sugar regulation, reduced harmful blood fats, and helped obese animals lose fat without a significant reduction in lean muscle mass. It also increased energy expenditure by up to 18%, even though the mice did not become more physically active or experience an increase in body temperature.

The findings, published in Science Advances, suggest a promising fresh direction for treating obesity, diabetes, and fatty liver disease. The experimental compound also appeared to enhance the benefits of popular weight-loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy when the treatments were used together. However, its effectiveness and safety have not yet been established in humans.

A Different Approach to Weight Loss Than Ozempic.

Over the past five years, medications known as GLP-1 drugs have transformed the treatment of obesity and other metabolic conditions, including diabetes and fatty liver disease. Drugs marketed as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound have helped many patients achieve substantial weight loss while improving their ability to regulate blood sugar.

It has been revealed that despite these benefits, the medications have key limitations. Nausea and other digestive problems can make treatment difficult for some patients. Because these drugs reduce appetite and food consumption, they can also increase the risk of inadequate nutrition and loss of muscle mass. Over time, losing too much muscle can contribute to weakness, frailty, and other health complications.

In a recent development, berkeley researchers wanted to investigate a fundamentally different strategy. Rather than focusing on reducing calorie intake, they explored whether it would be possible to increase the amount of energy the body burns.

This process, known as energy expenditure, includes the calories used to maintain basic bodily functions, regulate metabolism, and support everyday activities. Increasing energy expenditure could potentially help people lose weight without relying exclusively on eating less.

"Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," noted Anders Näär, a professor of metabolic biology and nutrition at UC Berkeley and senior author of the study. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second.".

A Compound That Burns Fat While Preserving Muscle.

The researchers focused on a molecule called 5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid (TOFA), which has an unusual combination of effects on the body's metabolism.

Sources indicate that TOFA interferes with the production of lipids, a broad category of fatty substances that includes cholesterol and triglycerides. These molecules serve important functions, but excessive levels of certain lipids can contribute to metabolic disorders and cardiovascular disease.

Sources indicate that at the same time, TOFA activates genes involved in taking up and burning fat for energy. This combination allows the compound to influence both how the body produces fat and how it uses fat as fuel.

Recent findings suggest that in mice, treatment with TOFA produced several encouraging results. The animals became more sensitive to insulin, the hormone that helps move glucose from the bloodstream into cells. Improved insulin sensitivity makes it easier for the body to control blood sugar, an important benefit for people with diabetes or insulin resistance.

The compound also lowered triglyceride levels and improved characteristics of fatty liver disease, a condition in which excess fat accumulates inside liver cells and can eventually interfere with liver function.

Perhaps most notably, obese mice treated with TOFA lost weight primarily through reductions in body fat, without experiencing significant losses of lean muscle mass. This distinction could be especially valuable because maintaining muscle is crucial for strength, mobility, and long-term metabolic health.

How TOFA Increases Energy Burning by 18%.

Although TOFA was originally discovered in the 1970s, the new research uncovered additional properties that could make it particularly useful for treating metabolic disease.

According to recent reports, the compound belongs to a group of substances known as ACC inhibitors. These compounds interfere with enzymes that help the body manufacture fatty acids, effectively slowing the production of certain fats.

Recent findings suggest that other ACC inhibitors have previously advanced to mid-stage clinical trials, but none has been approved to treat metabolic diseases. One major obstacle has been an unexpected side effect: many of these compounds increase triglycerides in the blood, potentially raising the risk of heart problems.

The Berkeley team discovered that TOFA does more than inhibit ACC. It also activates two cellular receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which help regulate the genes responsible for fat metabolism.

These receptors function as molecular switches. When activated, they stimulate processes that allow cells to absorb fatty acids and break them down to produce energy. In effect, TOFA simultaneously reduces the production of certain fats and encourages the body to burn fat that is already available.

In mice, this activity increased energy expenditure by as much as 18%, without requiring additional physical activity or raising body temperature. Unlike other ACC inhibitors, TOFA also did not cause triglyceride levels to rise, potentially because of its additional effects on fat metabolism.

"TOFA appears to engage a coordinated metabolic response," stated study first author Justin Y. Lee, a postdoctoral student at UCSF who conducted the research as a Ph.D. student at Berkeley. "It is not simply blocking lipid synthesis. It is also activating energy expenditure pathways that may help the body handle excess lipid and glucose more effectively.".

Sources indicate that to understand whether these effects could be reproduced with separate treatments, the scientists gave mice a combination of two different compounds. One blocked lipid production, while the other stimulated energy expenditure.

Sources indicate that surprisingly, this two-compound approach was less effective at improving overall metabolic health than TOFA alone. The finding suggests that TOFA's ability to influence multiple metabolic processes through a single molecule may be an crucial part of its effectiveness.

Could TOFA Make Ozempic and Wegovy More Effective?

The researchers also investigated whether TOFA could improve the results of existing GLP-1 medications.

They tested the compound alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, as well as tirzepatide, which is marketed as Mounjaro and Zepbound.

These medications primarily help people lose weight by reducing appetite and food intake. TOFA, by contrast, targets the other side of the energy balance equation by increasing how much energy the body expends.

When the researchers combined TOFA with these medications in mice, the results were more favorable than those produced by either treatment alone. The combinations led to greater improvements in body weight, blood glucose regulation, insulin levels, and triglycerides.

This suggests that treatments targeting calorie intake and energy expenditure could potentially work together to produce stronger metabolic benefits.

"In our combination experiments, TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs, so we view it as complementary rather than as a replacement," Näär stated.

Industry observers note that in other words, the researchers do not necessarily envision TOFA replacing medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy. Instead, it could eventually become an additional treatment that helps address obesity and related metabolic conditions through a different biological mechanism.

A Promising Discovery, but Human Trials Are Still Needed.

Industry observers note that despite the encouraging results, the researchers emphasize that TOFA remains an experimental compound. All the findings so far come from animal studies, and scientists have not yet established whether it is safe or effective in humans.

Further research will be necessary to determine whether the same metabolic improvements can be achieved in people and whether the treatment could offer meaningful advantages over existing medications.

Industry observers note that to help move the research toward potential clinical applications, the Berkeley scientists have established a biotechnology company called ReRx Therapeutics. The effort has received support from the university's life sciences entrepreneurship network, including Nucleate and Berkeley SkyDeck.

Sources indicate that if the findings eventually translate to humans, TOFA could represent an vital addition to the growing range of treatments for obesity and diabetes. By encouraging the body to use more energy while helping preserve muscle, the compound points toward a potentially different way to achieve healthier weight loss.

The research was funded through discretionary resources provided by UC Berkeley, with additional support from the UCSF Liver Center and the University of Michigan Animal Phenotyping Core.

Additional authors include Chi Zhu, Melissa A. Boldridge, Rachelle L. Stark, Lei Xu, Federico Gonzalez, Xin Tang, Kaitlyn T. Dang and Kook Son of Berkeley; Gracia Bonilla, Kashish Chetal and Ruslan I. Sadreyev of Massachusetts General Hospital; Kosuke Watari and Michael Karin of the University of California, San Diego; Christina Papa and Bilal N. Sheikh of the Helmholtz Center Munich; Prabha Ibrahim of ReRx Therapeutics.

Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel capzized off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities noted on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, noted in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it capsized about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

According to Spanish authorities, the Med Emre was drifting upside down northwest of Ibiza after capsizing. Initially, they remarked the ship had sunk to the seabed in 1,000 metres of water, but later corrected this statement.

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the incident was not immediately clear.

Sources indicate that the Transport Ministry noted the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency strategy at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government noted it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable.".

But he mentioned the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood.".

It has been revealed that "It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he remarked.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.

#150830. Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1121 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite.
  • The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution.
  • Sources indicate that that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the human family tree may be due for a major rewrite. Upcoming research from Monash University challenges the traditional way scientists classify our ancient ancestors, suggesting that several groups long considered separate from humans may actually belong within our own genus, Homo.

The study, published in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology, proposes a sweeping change to how we organize millions of years of human evolution. Its central argument is that all human species and their closely related fossil relatives from the past 4 to 5 million years should be classified within the genus Homo.

Sources indicate that that would mean bringing groups such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus, which have traditionally been classified separately, into the same genus as modern humans. Although these ancient relatives differed considerably in appearance, anatomy, and behavior, the researchers argue that the evolutionary boundaries separating them are becoming increasingly difficult to justify.

Why the Human Family Tree May Need to Be Redrawn.

Human evolution is frequently illustrated as a relatively orderly progression, beginning with ancestors that resembled apes and gradually moving through species such as Australopithecus and early Homo before arriving at modern humans, Homo sapiens.

Recent findings suggest that however, evolution did not unfold as a simple sequence in which one species neatly replaced another. Instead, the fossil evidence reveals a complicated family tree with numerous branches, overlapping species, and evolutionary relationships that scientists are still working to understand.

Each newly introduced fossil discovery can complicate that picture. Traits once believed to distinguish one group of ancient human relatives from another have increasingly been found across multiple groups, making it harder to determine where traditional classifications should begin and end.

Dr. Ian Towle, a Research Fellow at the Monash Biomedicine Discovery Institute and lead researcher on the study, argues that these discoveries are exposing weaknesses in the existing classification system. This applies not only to species already assigned to Homo, but also to members of Australopithecus and Paranthropus, groups that lived during the past 5 million years.

"Recent fossil discoveries and advances in evolutionary and genetic analysis make this an ideal time to reconsider whether our traditional taxonomy still accurately reflects human evolution," Dr. Towle stated.

"These groups do not necessarily represent distinct evolutionary branches, or 'clades', and differences in behavior and ecology once used to distinguish them have also become increasingly difficult to maintain.

"I propose expanding Homo to include these other groups to provide a more accurate and stable way to represent the complex evolutionary relationships revealed by the growing fossil record.".

How Scientists Classify Our Ancient Ancestors.

To understand the proposed change, it helps to look at how scientists organize living and extinct organisms.

The system is known as taxonomy, which involves naming species and arranging them into groups based on their characteristics and evolutionary relationships.

It has been revealed that A genus is one level of this system, sitting above the species level. Modern humans, for example, belong to the species Homo sapiens, with Homo identifying our genus and sapiens identifying our species.

Over the past 50 years, advances in evolutionary research have significantly changed how scientists approach classification. Rather than relying primarily on physical similarities, modern taxonomy increasingly seeks to organize species according to their actual evolutionary ancestry.

According to recent reports, an important concept in this approach is the clade. A clade consists of a common ancestor and all of its descendants. By grouping organisms this way, scientists aim to produce classifications that accurately reflect the branches of the evolutionary tree.

This approach has become increasingly influential in biology over recent decades. However, Towle argues that the classification of our own evolutionary relatives has been slower to adopt these principles consistently.

Why Brain Size and Tool Use No Longer Define Humans.

Traditionally, scientists have distinguished members of the genus Homo from other ancient human relatives using a combination of physical and behavioral characteristics.

These have included relatively large brains, sophisticated tool use, and particular anatomical features associated with human evolution.

But discoveries over recent decades have challenged the reliability of those distinctions.

Scientists have identified members of Homo with surprisingly small brains, demonstrating that a large brain was not necessarily a defining characteristic of every species in our genus.

At the same time, evidence suggests that species traditionally placed in Australopithecus and Paranthropus likely displayed more complex behaviors than researchers once assumed.

It has been revealed that together, these findings have weakened the boundaries used to separate the three groups. Characteristics once thought to be exclusive to Homo may have been shared more widely among our ancient relatives.

As a result, determining which species belong within the human genus has become increasingly complicated. Towle argues that the problem may lie not with the fossil evidence, but with the classification system scientists are trying to fit it into.

A Radical Proposal for 5 Million Years of Human Evolution.

Towle's proposed solution is to expand the genus Homo to include species at the moment classified as Australopithecus and Paranthropus.

According to recent reports, the idea is not that these ancient relatives were identical to modern humans or possessed all the traits associated with our species. Rather, the broader classification would recognize their evolutionary connections while still allowing scientists to distinguish among individual species.

It has been revealed that such a change could also make human taxonomy more stable. Instead of repeatedly revising the boundaries between major groups whenever fresh fossils are uncovered, scientists could use a broader genus that accommodates the diversity revealed by ongoing discoveries.

Sources indicate that the proposal represents a significant departure from traditional classifications, and it remains a scientific argument rather than an officially adopted change. Nevertheless, it highlights how much our understanding of human origins has evolved as fresh evidence has accumulated.

"The more we learn about our ancestors and close fossil relatives, the more we realize how complex and non-linear our family tree is," Dr. Towle said.

"Expanding the Homo genus to also include species of Australopithecus and Paranthropus will allow us to account for differences without regularly reclassifying particular groups.".

Ultimately, the research raises a fundamental question about how scientists define the human family. If the traits once used to separate our ancestors are not as distinctive as previously believed, the names and categories used to describe millions of years of human evolution may need to change along with our understanding of the past.
